en: The Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the village of Varṇasaṃcaya on Mount Himavat.
In the Golden Adorned Cave,
together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering exactly one thousand,
the World-Honored One then donned his robes and took up his alms bowl.
He entered the village of exquisite forms to wander for alms everywhere;
having returned to his original place and finished his meal,
he sat cross-legged, unmoving with right mindfulness.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi named "The Equal Characteristic of All Dharmas.
Having entered this samādhi,
the bhikṣus and others prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Suddenly, they could no longer see where the Tathāgata was;
they asked one another,
"Where has the Bhagavān Sugata gone now?"
At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven and the thirty-three gods,
empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, came to where the Buddha was.
Then there were also the King of the Śakra Heaven and the King of the Brahmā Heaven.
He formed this thought:
"Where is the Bhagavān now? Where is the Sugata now? Having thus brought mindfulness to the body, he reflected.
He beheld the Buddha’s body dwelling within a golden cave, having entered into samādhi.
At that time, the Śakras and devas came to the Buddha’s location and sat in silence.
The various assemblies of devas, including those of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven,
also sat in silence. At that time,
the World-Honored One manifested various supernormal powers within samādhi.
By the power of the Buddha’s supernormal faculties,
all those in the three thousandfold world system who study the Bodhisattva vehicle and have first resolved their minds upon awakening—
Or again, there were those who had long since resolved upon bodhicitta,
those who were non-retrogressive (avaivartika),
and those who were in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).
Because they had attained the Tathāgata’s teaching on supernatural powers,
they came to the Buddha’s presence at the聚落 (village) of *Miaose* (Exquisite Color).
It was by the Buddha’s spiritual power that this occurred.
He remained seated cross-legged at a height of one blade above the ground.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī entered the Samādhi of Delighting All Sentient Beings.
Having entered samādhi,
he caused the great assembly to attain joy in their hearts and experience delight in their minds.
They attained peace of mind and a sense of rare wonder.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
He entered the samādhi of the tranquil concentration on all phenomena.
Having entered this samādhi,
he caused the faculties of the entire great assembly to become tranquil and settled.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Lakṣaṇa,
together with sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas,
proceeded toward the Gold-Adorned Cave in the village of Varṇa.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling,
he saw himself and all the bodhisattvas abiding in the void,
sitting cross-legged in mid-air.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
together with ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas,
descended from the midst of the sky toward the Gold-Adorned Cave in the village of Varṇa.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, they were unable to descend to the ground;
together with the bodhisattvas, they remained in the air in the full lotus posture and immediately entered the samādhi that shatters and disperses the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Once he had entered samādhi,
all the members of that great assembly immediately extinguished their afflictions, including greed, desire, and delusion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnalakṣaṇa...
He immediately entered the Great Adornment Samādhi.
Having entered this samādhi,
he caused blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka) to rain down everywhere throughout space.
It eclipsed the light of the sun.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upright in samādhi, ascended into the void, and smiled with joy.
He even emitted rays of light in blue, yellow, red, white, gold, and crystal.
It was likewise so.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī stood in the air,
with palms joined, kneeling long, and adjusting his robes.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do you smile with such joy?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"I recall that in the past,
ten thousand Buddhas were here in this empty space."
In this very place, he taught the Dharma-gate of the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One, we pray that the Tathāgata will once again analyze and explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the dharma of the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
There is no need to say more:
within this Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī,
there is neither affliction nor nirvāṇa.
When they desire to enter nirvāṇa,
within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither the dharma of bodhisattvas nor the dharmas of the Buddhas.
Those who wish to attain Buddhahood [should know that] within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there are neither wholesome dharmas nor unwholesome dharmas.
In order to abandon those unwholesome states,
within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither this shore nor the further shore.
Those who wish to reach the other shore will find that within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is no one who has not accomplished the Buddha-fields.
For those who wish to accomplish the various Buddha-fields,
within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither Māra nor even the name of Māra.
In that *Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī*, which they desire to bring down upon all Māras,
there are no śrāvakas nor even the name of "śrāvaka."
They wish to transcend the Śrāvaka-dharma;
within the Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī,
there is neither Pratyekabuddha nor Pratyekabuddha-dharma.
Desiring to transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddhas,
they find within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī that there are no sentient beings, nor even the names of sentient beings.
When they wish to transform all sentient beings,
within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither benefit nor harm.
Those who seek profit [find that] within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither desire nor even the name of "desire."
Those who wish to be free from desire [should know that] within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither the name of "affliction" nor "one who is afflicted."
In order to be free from affliction,
within that Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī,
there is neither delusion nor even the name of delusion.
In order to abandon delusion,
they [state] within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī:
"There is neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom."
In their desire to realize wisdom,
within the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is neither affliction nor the absence of affliction.
There is neither purity nor impurity;
there is neither informative action nor non-informative action;
there is no loving-kindness, no compassion, no sympathetic joy, and no equanimity.
There is no giving and no stinginess;
no precepts and no transgressions;
no contention and no patience.
There is no progress and no regression;
there is no meditative concentration and no distracted mind;
there is no wisdom and no absence of wisdom.
There is no falling away;
there are no śrāvakas and no pratyekabuddhas;
there are no buddhas and no tathāgatas.
There is neither dharma nor non-dharma;
neither depth nor shallowness;
neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
There is no name and no place of realization;
there is no affliction and no nirvana;
there are no powers.
There are no factors of enlightenment;
there are no faculties;
there are no foundations of mindfulness.
There is no state of right concentration;
there are no four bases of psychic power, Mañjuśrī.
If one practices and attains the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
one does not abandon the dharmas of an ordinary person.
Neither grasping nor clinging, nor yet distancing oneself;
neither establishing anything,
nor needing to transcend.
Neither realizing nor abandoning;
neither contemplating abandonment nor excelling or emerging.
He is free from indolence; he does not feel aversion, nor does he harbor resentment, nor does he experience regret, nor does he encounter provocation.
Within the dharmas of ordinary beings, he does not give rise to afflictions.
All acts of giving are performed without forming signs of giving or signs of bestowing;
nor does one abandon the qualities of all Buddhas,
nor does one come into contact with the qualities of ordinary worldlings.
The dharmas of all Buddhas are not separate from the dharmas of ordinary beings;
the dharmas of ordinary beings are not separate from the dharmas of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, they do not establish the dharmas of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Nor does it reside within the dharmas of the Buddhas;
it does not abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings,
nor does it grasp at the protection of those dharmas of ordinary beings.
One must not remain motionless within the buddha-fields;
one must not abandon the great vows, Mañjuśrī.
Within this Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī,
there is no discrimination. Why is this so?
The phenomena of desire, hatred, and delusion are all equal,
for male and female are the same.
This applies equally to devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.
Because all phenomena are equal in their characteristics of differentiation;
because the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the śrāvakas,
and the pratyekabuddhas are all equally identical within all phenomena.
Because the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals are equal and identical;
because the element of water, the element of wind, the element of fire, the element of earth, and the element of space are equal and identical;
and because all phenomena are equal and identical.
Because the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, up to all phenomena, are equal and identical. Mañjuśrī,
this is the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī.
For example, it is like all the space that exists in the eastern direction,
all the space that exists in the southern, western,
and northern directions, and all the space that exists in the zenith and nadir.
They are all entirely equal and identical.
That is to say, they are of one essence, equal like space.
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī.
This is the Dharma of the Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī.
Because all sentient beings are equal and identical,
having spoken these words, [he remained silent].
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One,
in what way is desire a dhāraṇī phrase?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Desire does not come from the east to afflict sentient beings;
nor does it come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below to afflict sentient beings."
Nor does it emerge from within,
nor does it come from without to afflict sentient beings, Mañjuśrī.
If desire arises within and afflicts sentient beings,
those beings will never attain purity,
nor will they be able to realize the true nature of all phenomena.
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena neither go nor come; they are neither internal nor external, and have no place of abiding.
Therefore, this is called the dhāraṇī phrase.
“Mañjuśrī, ‘affliction’ is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what way is ‘affliction’ a dhāraṇī phrase?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
Affliction arises from contention;
that contention is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present.
Mañjuśrī, if past dharmas were indestructible once produced, they would have to be eternal dharmas.
Mañjuśrī, regarding future conditions, no affliction can arise;
as for present conditions...
Because they have no abiding place and because they are subject to disintegration, Mañjuśrī,
all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Furthermore, there is no future or present birth;
this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the purity of the three periods of time, Mañjuśrī.
Ignorance is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
"What is the meaning of delusion as a dhāraṇī phrase?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"Delusion arises from ignorance."
They do not rely on the earth element, nor the water element, nor the fire element, nor the wind element, nor the space element;
even unto the consciousness element, all phenomena are without any basis for attachment.
It cannot be afflicted, nor can it be purified.
Why? Because its essence is non-attachment.
One cannot be afflicted, nor can one be purified.
If those dharmas whose essence is non-attachment could be afflicted or purified,
then even space should be capable of being afflicted or purified.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī, space does not serve as a basis for any phenomena.
All ignorance has no place of attachment and no place of transition.
It has no place of destruction; it has no place of manifestation;
it is unobstructed and invisible.
Because it is without bondage, without liberation, boundless, and without intrinsic nature—
can such space be said to be afflicted or purified?
Mañjuśrī said, "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
Regarding "ignorance" (avidyā):
as the Tathāgata has taught,
it is called ignorance because it is fundamentally non-existent from the very beginning.
This phrase "ignorance" cannot be apprehended in the past limit;
it cannot be apprehended in the future limit.
The present limit is also unattainable.
Mañjuśrī, of all dharmas, there is nothing that exists.
That which cannot be apprehended,
that which cannot be seen,
and that for which there is no knower.
"Are they able to liberate or bind?
Can they also create obstacles? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No, Blessed One. No, Sugata. If such were the meaning."
"How is it, World-Honored One?
Does ignorance give rise to affliction?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī," [he replied].
For example, when two pieces of wood and human effort come together and rub against one another, fire is produced.
That fiery heat does not arise from the two pieces of wood alone,
nor does it arise from human effort alone.
And yet they are able to be born.
In this way, in this way, Mañjuśrī.
Because there is no right concentration, the afflictions of desire, the afflictions of anger, and the afflictions of delusion arise.
Those various afflictions do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two.
In this way, Mañjuśrī, regarding what is called "affliction":
how does it arise, and what is termed "delusion"?
All phenomena are originally liberated.
Because they can give rise to affliction, they are called delusion.
All phenomena are originally liberated.
"There is no place of bondage;
therefore, delusion is called the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, is there perhaps a single dharma which,
once a bodhisattva has practiced it, enables them to enter all dhāraṇīs and all gateways to the Dharma?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "There is a Dharma-gate of illumination consisting of a single syllable.
Once a bodhisattva has attained it, they are able to expound Dharma-gates of ten million syllables;
yet this Dharma-gate of a single syllable is itself inexhaustible."
In every place and at every time, he expounds the characteristics of all phenomena without limit;
when one attains this illumination of all phenomena, [one realizes them].
They naturally attain unimpeded eloquence;
all phenomena are inexhaustible. Having thus expounded upon all phenomena, [he said:]
They further subsume [all teachings] into the dharma-gate of a single word;
because they have attained unimpeded eloquence,
they are able to extensively expound a single phrase of the dharma-gate.
Having thus explained the increase and further increase,
[the teaching] is again subsumed within a single dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the Dharma-gate of a single word?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"There is not a single dharma whatsoever;
this is called the Dharma-gate of the One-Syllable Dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called the dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī phrases?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas abide on the ground of subduing; therefore,
it is called the Dharma-gate of entering the *dhāraṇī* of subduing.
Mañjuśrī, the gate of the Dharma of the heavens— that is, all dharmas—
is called the gate of the dhāraṇī-dharma.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason is this Dharma-gate called 'The Celestial Dhāraṇī'?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, it is because all dharmas abide in the stage of cultivation."
This is called the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī of the Mutual Entry of the Names of the Devas. Mañjuśrī,
it is the Dharma-gate of the dragons and of all phenomena.
"This is the dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One,"
"For what reason is this Dharma-gate of dhāraṇī called 'Dragon'?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "It has no name."
All dharmas sever the path of names; because they are without characters yet are provisionally designated by characters,
it is called the Dharma-gate of the Dragon-Entry Dhāraṇī Characters.
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas, including the dharma-gates of yakṣas,
are this dhāraṇī dharma-gate.
For what reason is this dhāraṇī dharma-gate called "yakṣa"?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Because it is the characteristic of exhaustion."
Mañjuśrī, because all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, this is called the yakṣa dhāraṇī dharma-gate.
All dharmas are the dharma-gate of the gandharva. Why is it called the dharma-gate of the gandharva dhāraṇī?
Because numbers are infinite,
all dharmas have no limit; it is only by taking the limit of space as a reference that they are so designated.
The characteristic of the gandharva is called the dharma-gate of entering dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī,
all dharmas are the dharma-gate of the asuras.
Regarding this dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī, for what reason is it called "Asura"?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas have no fixed abode;
they cannot be expressed by means of names.
That which is not form cannot be practiced as something other than the characteristic of form;
that which is not sound cannot be practiced as something other than the characteristic of sound;
that which is not fragrance cannot be practiced as something other than the characteristic of fragrance.
It is not the case that flavor can proceed as something other than the characteristic of flavor;
it is not the case that tangibility can proceed as something other than the characteristic of tangibility;
it is not the case that the mind can proceed as something other than the characteristic of the mind.
That which is not the Buddha cannot be practiced as something other than the characteristics of the Buddha;
that which is not the Dharma cannot be practiced as something other than the characteristics of the Dharma;
that which is not the Sangha cannot be practiced as something other than the characteristics of the Sangha.
It is not the case that one can practice as anything other than a śrāvaka, nor as anything other than the characteristics of a śrāvaka;
it is not the case that one can practice as anything other than a pratyekabuddha, nor as anything other than the characteristics of a pratyekabuddha;
it is not the case that one can practice as anything other than an ordinary person, nor as anything other than the characteristics of an ordinary person.
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are without the characteristic of activity, and there is no characteristic of that which is to be practiced, nor of the practice itself.
Because there is no arousal [of thought],
this is called the *dhāraṇī* dharma-gate of the asuras, Mañjuśrī.
All dharmas of the garuḍa-dharmaparyāya are this dhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is the garuḍa this dharanī dharma-gate?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
All phenomena have neither coming nor going; thus, there is no coming,
yet it is not that there is no coming.
There is no going and no non-going;
it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither leaking nor clinging, neither bound nor liberated;
it is neither defiled nor false, and there is no place for defilement or attachment.
They abide without establishment, because from the very beginning they have been without establishment. Mañjuśrī,
all phenomena are thus.
Because it is like space, having no basis,
it is called the *dhāraṇī* dharma-gate of the entry of the garuḍa, Mañjuśrī.
"Kinnara, all dharmas are this dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is this dharani-dharmaparyāya called ‘Kinnara’?
The Buddha said:
Because it is free from the path of action, Mañjuśrī,
that which is unconditioned and the agent are both non-existent.
This is called the mark of the kiṃnara; it is the dharma-gate for entering dhāraṇīs.
Mañjuśrī, such is the dharma-gate of the mahoragas regarding all phenomena.
"This is the dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One..."
"What is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
'All phenomena are free from defilement and are originally luminous and pure.'"
This dharma-gate of the pure dhāraṇī cannot be defiled nor can it be purified by any sentient beings.
Why is that? Mañjuśrī, all dharmas...
Because they are originally quiescent and because they are originally unarisen, Mañjuśrī.
This is called the Dharma-gate for entering the dhāraṇī of the mahoragas. Mañjuśrī,
this Dharma-gate of women encompasses all dharmas.
"This is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī asked, "What is this dharma-gate of dhāraṇī?"
The Buddha said, "Because they are false and illusory. Mañjuśrī,
because all dharmas lack fixed female or male organs."
Because it is not a substantial entity,
it is called the Dharani-dharma-gate of Entering the Characteristics of Women, Mañjuśrī.
“Sons of noble family, all dharmas are this dharma-gate of dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said:
"What is this dharma-gate of dhāraṇī?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,"
Because the characteristics of all places do not exist,
they cannot be apprehended from the beginning limit (pūrvakoṭi) onward,
nor can they be apprehended even at the subsequent limit (aparākoṭi).
The present, too, cannot be apprehended.
Mañjuśrī, this is because the three time periods are non-apprehendable.
In this place there is neither male nor female; it is spoken of only by way of conventional designation.
That which is called "designation" receives its name because it is vast and extensive.
Those forms (rūpa) are composed of the combination of the four great elements (mahābhūta).
Because these phenomena have no place of arising and are quiescent from the very beginning, Mañjuśrī.
"All dharmas" is the name for the dharma-gate of the *dhāraṇī* of entering the male characteristic. Mañjuśrī,
all dharmas are the dharma-gate of hell.
"This is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One,"
"For what reason is the hell named the Dharani Dharma-gate?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "What kind of characteristics does the entrance to hell possess?"
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
those in the hells enter into the mark of empty space."
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī, what do you think?"
As for hell-beings:
do they arise from one's own conceptual discrimination,
or do they arise spontaneously?
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
it is because these ordinary persons give rise to conceptual discrimination."
One sees the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts;
yet these have no reality,
and it is only ordinary beings who undergo suffering and affliction therein.
World-Honored One,
according to what I see,
there is no perception of hell.
"There is no perception of suffering,
World-Honored One.
It is like a person who, while asleep, dreams of falling into hell."
He sees himself within a great boiling cauldron,
along with immeasurable people undergoing various agonies;
as heat and distress oppress his body, he gives rise to great terror.
He was immediately seized with great alarm and cried out;
suddenly he began to chant, "Great suffering!
Great suffering! wailing and sobbing until his voice failed him.
The person's parents and kinsmen asked,
"What suffering do you have?
The person replied:
"I have fallen into hell and am suffering; how can you ask me what pain I have?"
Then his parents and all his kinsmen said to that man,
"Do not be afraid."
"You merely saw this while asleep.
You did not go outside of your dwelling while asleep;
why then do you suddenly say that you are undergoing the sufferings of hell?"
That person immediately regains their lucid mind and realizes:
"What I have seen was merely a dream.
Thus does he perceive within his own inner mind.
All these were not real, yet they still experienced joy.
World-Honored One,
it is like that person in a dream who, though there was no actual reality, saw himself falling into hell.
"So it is, so it is, World-Honored One.
All ordinary beings originally have no desire."
They form the conceptualization of them as women;
they enjoy each other's company and naturally give rise to attachment and pleasure.
They then think to themselves:
"I am male and she is female. Having given rise to a mind of desire,
he immediately seeks the five objects of desire for the sake of those five desires.
They engage in mutual strife and contention, forming various enmities;
they squander their wealth and property, and further inflict harm upon one another,
giving rise to perverted views and thoughts of resentment and hatred.
"World-Honored One, after dying, that person enters hell for many thousands of kalpas,
just as if it were a dream."
All their parents and kinsmen said to that person,
"You have not yet emerged from sleep;
how is it that you see yourself undergoing the sufferings of hell?"
"So it is, so it is, World-Honored One.
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas..."
For the sake of sentient beings who are subject to the four perversions,
he preaches the True Dharma;
yet in this state, there is no male, no female, and no sentient being.
There is no experiencer, no nourisher,
and neither a pudgala nor a self.
All these dharmas are inverted;
because they originally do not exist, these dharmas arise;
because of their conjunction, these dharmas arise.
These phenomena arise through conceptual differentiation;
they have no place of origination.
These phenomena possess no substantial entity.
These phenomena do not adhere to one another;
these phenomena are like dreams;
these phenomena are like illusions.
These dharmas are like the moon in water;
these dharmas have no place of attachment;
these dharmas have no defiler.
Those who are without affliction and without forgetfulness—
do not engage in false conceptualization regarding them.
These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma of the Tathāgata, [attain such states].
He immediately becomes weary of desire,
perceives the nature of all phenomena,
and distances himself from all afflictions.
They remain far removed from all delusion;
they see that all phenomena are primordially liberated,
and they see that all phenomena are without obstruction.
"World-Honored One, those people perceive all dharmas as quiescent."
Having attained the meditative absorption on space,
after casting off the body,
one enters parinirvāṇa within nirvana without remainder.
“World-Honored One,
I have seen the marks of suffering in the hells to be such as these.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!
It is just as you have seen it;
the hells should be viewed in this way.
One should also distinguish it in this way, as you have said:
having known and seen such hells.
He attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), just as Mañjuśrī had attained it.
Having spoken these words, [he remained silent].
Twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and,
with one voice, proclaimed:
"How rare is the sphere of activity of the Buddhas!"
That which is called "manifesting all Buddha-dharmas within the dharmas of the hells.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
I pray that you will explain for me the gateway to entering the non-dual dharma.
Having entered this gateway to the non-dual dharma,
may all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [be liberated] from within all afflictions.
They expound all the teachings of the Buddhas,
yet do not form dualistic conceptions;
furthermore, they attain unimpeded eloquence in their exposition.
"World-Honored One, all phenomena are without dual characteristics.
How does one enter the gateway to the non-dual dharma?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, listen attentively and receive this well; reflect upon it thoroughly."
I have taught you this dharma-gate of the non-dual equality of names.
Having attained this dharma-gate,
all bodhisattvas, amidst all afflictions and amidst all the Buddha-dharmas, [abide in equanimity].
It can bring about equanimity;
furthermore, it is the differentiation of all afflictions,
and is called the dharani-dharmaparyāya.
"I shall now speak of it. Mañjuśrī said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I pray that you will speak for me so that I may joyfully hear it.
Mañjuśrī, ignorance is bodhi; this is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī."
Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One,
in what way is ignorance a dharani-dharma-gate?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Because there is no illumination, it is called ignorance (avidyā).
Because of ignorance, therefore there is no arising."
Because there is no arising, there are no afflictions. Mañjuśrī,
that which is without afflictions is called bodhi.
Its intrinsic nature is pure;
it has no locus of attachment and no locus of arising. For this reason.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that the Tathāgata has constantly, throughout various sūtras,
extensively expounded the dharma-gate of the non-duality of ignorance and bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, since the distant past, I have not found ignorance;
for this reason, [I am called the Tathāgata].
I speak of ignorance.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī of Ignorance.
Once the bodhisattva has attained this dharma-gate of wisdom,
they obtain swift eloquence and sharp eloquence.
They attain boundless eloquence.
They attain non-abiding eloquence, Mañjuśrī.
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are bodhi; this is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One, how is it that all conditioned phenomena are bodhi? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
The various conditioned formations exceed all number;
they cannot be grasped by calculation.
Therefore, one should contemplate the unwholesome states.
Being without limit, there is thus birth;
yet it does not depart from this place.
Nor does it come from elsewhere,
because there is neither coming nor going. Therefore, Mañjuśrī:
This is called the Dharma-gate of the *vidyā-dhāraṇī* for entering into the name of Bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, consciousness is Bodhi; this is the *dhāraṇī* Dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
how is it that consciousness is bodhi?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata has always taught that consciousness is like an illusion or a magical transformation."
They arise due to inversion.
Mañjuśrī said: "As for that which is illusory and conjured..."
It arises from conceptual discrimination;
it arises from the combination [of conditions];
because it relies on unreal conceptual discrimination.
These various marks of the illusory transformations of ordinary beings arise;
awakening arises from conceptual discrimination and arises from the coming together of conditions.
They manifest the dharmas of all Buddhas while remaining attached to the characteristics of phenomena, thinking:
"We shall become Buddhas in a future age;
we shall teach and transform all sentient beings."
"We shall attain that which is most supreme in the world," yet the characteristic of awakening is like space;
having given rise to such discrimination, they disparage others.
Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning,
I have never sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree;
such is the Dharma already attained by me.
Some are called Buddhas;
some are called Pratyekabuddhas;
and some are called Śrāvakas.
Or it is called "the ordinary person. Mañjuśrī,
for this reason, consciousness is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī, name-and-form is bodhi; it is a dharani-dharmaparyāya.
Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One,
why is it that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is called bodhi?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, as for 'name'— "
It is merely a conventional expression of sound and lacks any reality. Mañjuśrī,
as for "form":
There is no agent and no creator;
herein one cannot say that there is a self.
The absence of "mine" is itself bodhi. Mañjuśrī, this is called the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī of Entering the Characteristics of Form and Name.
Mañjuśrī, the six sense bases are bodhi; this is a dhāraṇī dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī, [this is so].
In this way, all such bases of cognition (*āyatana*) are each unfindable when sought within their respective activities.
The eye does not form the thought, "I see forms."
The ear does not form the thought, "I hear sounds.
The nose does not form the thought, "I smell odors.
The tongue does not form the thought, "I taste flavors."
The body does not form the thought, "I perceive touch";
the mind does not form the thought, "I cognize phenomena";
and the eye does not engage in the activity of knowing forms.
Form does not know the activity of the eye;
the ear does not know the activity of sound;
sound does not know the activity of the ear.
The nose does not know the activity of fragrance;
fragrance does not know the activity of the nose.
The tongue does not know the activity of taste.
The tongue does not know the activity of taste;
the body does not know the activity of touch;
touch does not know the activity of the body.
The mind does not know the activity of dharmas;
dharmas do not know the activity of the mind, Mañjuśrī.
The six sense bases are each mutually opposed;
all the sense bases are devoid of consciousness and are each without sensation.
Each and every thing is empty of its own intrinsic nature. Mañjuśrī,
the true characteristic of dharmas is truly empty.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the Dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī of the characteristics of the six sense bases. Mañjuśrī.
"Contact is bodhi; it is a dharani-dharmaparyaya.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One..."
"What is contact that is awakening?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "As for what is called 'contact'..."
These are the contact of form, the contact of sound, the contact of fragrance, the contact of taste, the contact of tangibles,
and the contact of mental phenomena. Mañjuśrī, as for all contacts of form:
That, then, has a condition.
If there is a condition,
it arises through discrimination and persists through the grasping of objective conditions.
Mañjuśrī said: "That which takes up objects of perception is like a magical illusion;
it is precisely a perversion."
If there is inversion, then there is non-existence;
if there is non-existence, then there is no arising;
if there is no arising, then there is no cessation. Because there is neither cessation nor arising, this is itself bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the dhāraṇī dharma-gate of the entrance of contact. Mañjuśrī.
"Receiving this is bodhi; it is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One..."
"What is feeling that is awakening?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"Feeling is of three kinds."
[There are] pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings. Mañjuśrī said:
"Feeling is neither internal, nor external, nor in between."
Mañjuśrī, whatever pleasure exists that is neither internal, nor external, nor in between—
that is non-existent.
“Mañjuśrī, how does one know that all sentient beings have attained the experience of happiness? Mañjuśrī replied:
World-Honored One,
because of inverted perceptions,
all ordinary beings falsely grasp at various conditions as either pleasant or painful.
"Venerable Sir, it is likewise when consciousness discriminates and knows that which is neither pleasant nor painful.
I see the nature of all feelings."
"Just as illusions and transformations are fundamentally unarisen," the Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"it is for this reason."
Mañjuśrī, one who understands the characteristics of sensation enters the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
"Affection is bodhi; it is a dhāraṇī dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One..."
"Is craving not the root of all afflictions?
The Buddha said,
"What do you think?"
It is like a person who has not yet had a child:
where does the heart of love for that child reside— is it within, without, or in some other place?
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
that person does not yet have a son."
"How can there be a mind that cherishes a son?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,"
At a later time, if that person conceives a child through union with a woman,
they will subsequently develop a heart of parental affection for that child.
What do you think? Does such a heart of parental love for one's child come from the east?
"Coming from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions,
and above and below— is he within or without? Mañjuśrī replied:
World-Honored One,
that mind of affection for one's child does not come from the ten directions, nor from within or without.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
regarding such craving,
who is its creator and who is its maker?"
Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One,
such is this craving.”
There is no one who creates it, nor is there any maker;
yet, due to the inverted conditions of ordinary worldlings,
they forcibly give rise to conceptual discrimination, and thus this craving exists.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī, if something lacks reality, can it be called existent? Mañjuśrī replied, "No,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
if phenomena do not exist,
can it be said that they have defilement or purity?"
Mañjuśrī said, “No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, if a dharma does not come from the ten directions, nor from within or without,
that dharma is neither defiled nor pure.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī for Entering the Characteristics of Craving. Mañjuśrī.
"Taking this up is the dharma-gate of bodhi and dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One," [he continued].
"How can grasping be awakening?
In the sūtras, the Tathāgata has never said that grasping is awakening.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī," [he continued].
“Do all ordinary beings possess grasping?
Mañjuśrī replied, “World-Honored One, they do.”
There is grasping.
One grasps at forms, grasps at sounds, grasps at odors, grasps at tastes, grasps at tangibles, and grasps at mental phenomena.
In this way, one grasps at the five objects of desire.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think? Is it possible to take up form by means of sound?"
“Does sound apprehend form?
Mañjuśrī replied, “No,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
is there even a single dharma that enters into all dharmas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
it is because all dharmas are unarisen."
Because they are without obstruction,
those phenomena cannot apprehend one another;
those phenomena cannot defile one another.
Nor can it be spoken of,
because all dharmas are fundamentally dull by nature, Mañjuśrī.
For this reason, Mañjuśrī,
you should know that grasping is itself awakening.
This is called the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī for Entering by Grasping Signs. Mañjuśrī,
this is the Bodhi that is this Dhāraṇī Dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for the sake of all śrāvakas to eliminate and extinguish all modes of existence."
"How is it that the Tathāgata now says that there is such a thing as bodhi?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,"
"Regarding 'existence' (bhava):
Mañjuśrī, I have indeed said that it is called 'existence' because it is the state of being far removed from all forms of existence."
Furthermore, if there is a person who perceives that all phenomena do not exist and does not perceive arising or ceasing.
He sees all existing entities as being like space.
One who sees in this manner does not take any buddha-dharmas as an object of attachment.
Nor does he abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings. Mañjuśrī,
it is for this reason.
"You should know that there is this bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī for Entering the Characteristic of Existence."
“Mañjuśrī, this awakening is the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said:
World-Honored One,
in the sutras of the Tathāgata, you have taught all sentient beings that they should distance themselves from the nature of arising.
Why, then, do you say that arising is bodhi?
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva wishes to seek a place of rebirth..."
One must contemplate the state where there is neither arising nor ceasing;
therein, one does not perceive such characteristics as arising and ceasing. For this reason:
Mañjuśrī, you should know that arising is bodhi.
If one can enter into this characteristic, [it is bodhi].
He attained swift eloquence, sharp eloquence, profound eloquence, peerless eloquence, unequaled eloquence, non-abiding eloquence, and inexhaustible eloquence.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
at what stage can a bodhisattva practice such profound dharmas as these?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva does not abide in bodhi and does not give rise to the thought of awakening, [he is a true bodhisattva].
They do not take the various Buddha-dharmas as an object of focus;
they do not establish various Buddha-fields;
and they do not distance themselves from greed, hatred, and delusion.
They do not transcend afflictions,
they do not transform sentient beings,
and they do not conceive of dualistic characteristics regarding any phenomena.
“Mañjuśrī, these bodhisattvas dwell in such a stage. Mañjuśrī said:
World-Honored One,
if there are people who can receive and uphold this Vajrapadadhāraṇī,
reciting and explaining it.
"How many kinds of merit does such a person obtain in the present life?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"If there is anyone who can receive and uphold this Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī..."
They shall read, recite, explain,
and constantly contemplate it in their minds so as not to let it be forgotten;
thus, in birth after birth and life after life, those people...
With a mind free from reviling the True Dharma, one attains fearlessness.
In this present life, devas, nāgas,
yakṣas, gandharvas, and others will constantly come to protect such a person.
He is always free from doubt regarding all the teachings of the Buddhas and attains the wisdom of discernment concerning all phenomena, Mañjuśrī.
I have briefly described the immeasurable and boundless merits of this dhāraṇī.
Were I to describe them in detail,
they could not be exhausted even in a thousand million kalpas.
When this Dharma-text of the dhāraṇī was being spoken,
ten thousand bodhisattvas attained this Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī;
furthermore, there were thirty thousand bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds toward enlightenment.
They attained the patient acceptance that accords with all dharmas.
When the Buddha had spoken this dharma of the dhāraṇī, the youth Mañjuśrī—
As well as the assembly of great bodhisattvas,
the assembly of śrāvakas, and the devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Having heard what the Buddha taught,
they prostrated at his feet and joyfully practiced it.
